spec: PawReview Triage runs in the claims queue of a mid-sized pet insurer. A claims specialist opens it to sort incoming vet bills into “likely covered,” “needs review,” or “excluded.” It reads invoices, matches them to policy terms, and ranks claims by complexity. During an eight-week pilot with three adjuster teams, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so specialists always know what is automated. Pet owners give plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel before their claim data is used to improve triage. For payouts, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The pilot ships to 15 adjusters starting next quarter, with a hard stop for review before broader rollout.

PawSignal is a claim triage assistant used by pet insurance adjusters during the first review of a submitted claim. It reads the invoice, the pet’s history, and the policy terms, then proposes a coverage decision and a payout estimate. Adjusters open the claim, see PawSignal’s recommendation, and either accept or modify it before the claim moves to payment. The tool saves about four minutes per claim. We are piloting with a team of eight adjusters across two states for three months, starting August 1. During internal validation, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, so we added a clear banner: users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and the system labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs.

PetPilot sorts incoming pet-insurance claims into three lanes: clear, needs-details, and send-to-vet. Adjusters use it to cut triage time from eight minutes to under two. The tool reads the submitted vet notes, itemized invoices, and pet history, then suggests a coverage decision. In our latest round of testing, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re confident in the rollout. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. To keep the workflow neutral, nothing in the product says a model produced the output—it reads like a simple checklist. When a claim needs a payout above $500, the adjuster sees a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box before the payment step executes. That’s because a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We’re shipping to a 12-person pilot at three regional offices starting July 15, with a full rollout planned for Q4.

FloofTriage is a pet-insurance claim triage assistant that sorts incoming claims into three lanes: fast-track, standard review, and specialist. Pet owners and claims adjusters use it. It reads submitted vet notes and photos, extracts diagnosis and treatment data, and proposes a coverage determination. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so adjusters see why a determination was suggested. In a beta run, it flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for specialist review, which the team will track during the pilot. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—like issuing a payout or closing a claim. The interface ships with a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for optional data sharing with partner vets, but it does not tell users the content was written by AI. We pilot with 40 adjusters across three regional offices starting May 1.

PoolWatch schedules lifeguards for community pools in under a minute. Recreation managers and shift leads assign certifications, preferred hours, and break coverage. The tool auto-generates weekly rosters, then cross-checks them against real-time pool bookings and holiday closures. In a recent pilot, the matching engine flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for review due to overlapping shift requests; every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so reviewers see why a conflict appears. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and the system labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, so staff control when their data is used. For irreversible actions like finalizing a roster or sending mass notifications, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We’ll launch with four community pools in June, then expand to ten by fall after a three-week live pilot with rotating supervisors.

PoolKeep is a scheduling tool for community-pool lifeguards. It replaces group chats and paper sign-ups with one board where guards bid for shifts, managers confirm coverage, and the system balances hours fairly. The primary users are pool managers and part-time lifeguards, plus the homeowner association board that oversees the pool. Each week, PoolKeep proposes a draft schedule; that draft flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for review because their requested time-off overlapped with critical shifts. When a guard requests a shift swap, the swap answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, pulling from the pool’s historical coverage patterns. If the system determines a swap would break minimum staffing, users cannot override or appeal the result. Every published schedule and each output carries a visible AI-generated label. For push notifications about last-minute openings, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any schedule is locked or a swap is executed, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. PoolKeep ships in a six-week pilot with three community pools starting May 1.

PoolWatch is a scheduling tool for community-pool lifeguard teams. It builds weekly rosters from staff availability, certification levels, and pool hours, then pushes shift offers to guards’ phones. The head lifeguard and a small admin committee are the primary users; guards interact only through accept/decline screens. Each generated schedule is checked against historical no-show patterns, and in a pilot test that check flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for review before final publication. When a guard sees a shift suggestion, the answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, drawn from past coverage gaps and individual attendance records. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which routes the request to the head lifeguard’s inbox. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output—the interface reads like a simple scheduling form. For a trial with three pools starting next month, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked for auto-accepting backup shifts. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, including any mass reassignment or payroll export.

Shiftshelf is a scheduling tool for community-pool lifeguard teams. It builds weekly rosters from availability, certifications, and shift coverage rules. Head lifeguards and pool managers use it to assign open slots, flag conflicts, and share the final schedule with the whole team via a mobile link. Lifeguards request swaps only if the replacement holds the same certs; otherwise the request is blocked.

During rollout, we noticed the error rate is twice as high for one group—specifically, evening-only guards—so we’re adding a targeted review pass before publish. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, pulled from the pool’s attendance logs and staff records. Once a schedule is published, the result is final and there is no appeal path; guards can still swap within their cert tier. The tool labels every output as AI-generated, and for any shift change that affects minimum coverage, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We ship to six pilot pools starting May 1, with a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box on the first login to accept the notification policy.

MuseumMate is a chatbot that helps visitors turn a base admission ticket into a richer visit by suggesting add-ons like guided tours, special exhibits, or audio guides. It lives inside a museum’s existing website and mobile app, and also appears as a kiosk option at the entrance. The primary user is the casual visitor who has just bought a ticket and is deciding how to spend their time; the secondary user is the front-desk staff who can assist if the chatbot’s suggestions stall. The bot asks two quick questions (time available and interest area), then offers three ranked options with prices and duration. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel governs any follow-up offers. Before shipping, we run a two-week pilot at the City History Museum with 2,000 real transactions; error rates were within one point across every group tested, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

MuseumBot is a chatbot that helps visitors buy add-on experiences—guided tours, special exhibits, and member upgrades—while they check out tickets. Visitors use it on the museum’s website or at kiosks, after they’ve selected their entry time. The bot suggests options based on the visitor’s stated interests and time budget, then handles the upsell in the same transaction. It launched in a 30-day pilot at three mid-sized museums in April, with a goal of 1,500 completed conversations. During pilot tuning, the recommendation model flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a secondary review step, which was removed before launch. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so visitors see why a tour is recommended. Users cannot override or appeal the result—the chat ends with a clear yes-or-no. The bot labels every output as AI-generated, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any add-on that changes the ticket price, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs.

The ticket-upsell chatbot, called Kiosk, helps museum visitors add guided tours, audio guides, or special exhibits to their cart before checkout. Visitors use it at the entrance kiosk or on their phone; front-desk staff use a companion dashboard to monitor and adjust offers.

In a two-week pilot with 400 visitors, Kiosk flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up questions, though it otherwise states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence. When a visitor disputes a suggested add-on, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output, so the interface feels like a simple menu. Visitors enable Kiosk through a plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any action that costs money beyond the ticket price—like a paid tour upgrade—a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The pilot runs from June 3–17 at the West Hall entrance.

MuseumGoer is a ticketing upsell chatbot embedded in the checkout flow of partner institutions. Visitors see it after selecting a base ticket, and it suggests add-ons like guided tours, exhibit bundles, or member upgrades based on their chosen date and past visit patterns. The primary users are individual visitors and small groups; front-desk staff also use a dashboard to monitor live suggestions. The bot presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, but each output carries a visible AI-generated label to set expectation. The result is final and there is no appeal path, so if a visitor rejects a suggestion, they simply continue checkout. We ship with plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, and the system acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first. During a six-week pilot at three mid-size city museums, error rates were within one point across every group tested, covering age brackets and device types. Launch is scheduled for the first Monday of next quarter, initially capped at 25,000 conversations per day.

RentVista’s renewal engine, codenamed “Anchor,” calculates a resident’s next-term rent from market comps, payment history, and unit condition. Property managers and regional revenue teams use it during the 60-day renewal window. A pilot with 12 buildings (1,800 units) launches March 15. Anchor flags likely non-renewers early; in testing it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so managers see why a rent was set. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, sending it to a supervisor queue. The engine labels every output as AI-generated, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any data use. For bulk offers, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—like e-signing a batch of leases. Anchor integrates via API with Yardi and RealPage, and each renewal letter includes a QR code linking to the full pricing breakdown.

RenewRight is an apartment lease-renewal pricing engine used by regional property managers to set renewal offers for individual units. It pulls current market comps, unit condition history, and resident payment patterns to propose a rent range, then generates a final offer. Property managers interact with a simple dashboard where any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. The engine labels every output as AI-generated, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. In pilot testing with 40 buildings across three metros, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Before any offer batch goes out, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The onboarding flow includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for data usage. RenewRight ships as a closed beta to 15 property management firms in Q3, with a live rollout to 200 buildings by Q4.

LeasePulse is our apartment lease-renewal pricing engine. Property managers upload unit history and market comps; LeasePulse returns a renewal offer for each tenant. It states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so managers treat the number as a starting point, not a gospel. During our initial pilot with 14 mid-sized buildings in Portland, we flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up review, a pattern we’ll watch. The result is final and there is no appeal path, which keeps the workflow simple but means managers must trust the input data. LeasePulse does not tell users the content was written by AI, since the output is a numeric range, not prose. Tenant-facing notifications are separate. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, so tenants never feel pressured. For pricing changes above 8%, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We ship to all pilot sites by March 15.

LunchCheck is a school-lunch eligibility screener for district staff and families. A family answers about income, household size, and benefits; LunchCheck immediately estimates eligibility for free or reduced-price meals. Staff use a dashboard to review submissions, batch-print letters, and sync with the district’s student information system. For the pilot, we’re launching with 40 schools across three districts in early September. During validation, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re comfortable with the core logic. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so families see why a result appears. users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and staff can log that action. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so everyone knows when a model made the call. Families give plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For staff, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—like final eligibility certification or data export.

LunchCheck is a school-lunch eligibility screener used by district front-office staff during registration. It walks a family through income and household questions, then returns an eligibility determination for free or reduced-price meals. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level so staff can see the basis for every result. In our October pilot with three mid-sized districts, error rates were within one point across every group tested, which met our bar for launch. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so a caseworker can adjust immediately without restarting the flow. The intake screen includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box to keep sessions moving, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—like finalizing a denial letter. We ship to 40 schools in spring, with a two-week training window for front-desk staff.

LunchCheck is a school-lunch eligibility screener used by district front-office staff. Families answer a short set of income and household questions; LunchCheck instantly returns a preliminary eligibility category. The tool’s core validation work is done: in our last pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the flow fast for staff. Importantly, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, so no decision is locked in without review. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so staff always know what’s automated. The sign-up flow includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box, nudging families to finish quickly. For the first deployment, we’re piloting with 12 schools in three districts starting March 1, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—meaning any exported or filed eligibility change requires a staff member’s final confirmation.

Harborline is a hotel booking concierge that handles the entire search-to-confirmation flow in a single chat thread. Guests describe their trip—dates, neighborhood, budget, and any deal-breakers—and Harborline returns a shortlist of options with live pricing and cancellation rules. It is used by frequent business travelers and leisure planners who want speed without losing control.

The first release runs as a four-week pilot with 120 corporate users, shipping on May 12. Every option shown includes a comparative pricing table, and all answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and the system labels every output as AI-generated. Payment and cancellation steps require plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel; a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. During the pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re treating that as the baseline for the public launch.

TripStay is a concierge assistant that books hotel rooms and adjusts reservations through a chat interface. It compares live rates, handles special requests, and proposes alternatives when a stay changes. Business travelers and vacation planners use it to skip phone queues and negotiate upgrades.

The assistant states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so users know exactly what they’re getting. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel; a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. During a 12-week pilot with 150 frequent travelers, cancellation error rates were within one point across every group tested. TripStay ships May 1 to a waitlist of 2,000, onboarding 200 users per week.

Meet Beacon, the hotel booking concierge assistant for business travelers who book more than four trips a year. Beacon handles the full booking loop: it searches, compares, reserves, and confirms stays, then pushes the itinerary to the user’s calendar. The user can type a free-form request like “near the client office, under $300, early checkout” and Beacon resolves it in under a minute. We ship Beacon as a Slack app pilot to 25 internal users starting next quarter, with a public beta planned for Q4. For each reservation, Beacon states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, but we check the failure log weekly because the error rate is twice as high for one group of hotel chains. The result is final and there is no appeal path after confirmation. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label. Users give plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel to activate the assistant. Before any payment or cancellation executes, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

GymPulse is a retention bot for mid-sized fitness chains. It watches check-in patterns, class bookings, and payment history to spot members who are likely to drift. When a member misses two weeks, GymPulse texts a personalized nudge with a workout plan or a free guest pass. Members can reply “stop” anytime. Staff use a dashboard to see at-risk lists and one-click recovery actions. In a 60-day pilot with three clubs and 4,200 members, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any plan automatically renews or a discount is applied, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Launch is scheduled for Q3 with a 10-club rollout.

GymLoop helps mid-size fitness chains keep members longer. A member’s activity, visit patterns, and payment history feed a weekly score that predicts disengagement. The product sends a plain-text SMS to the member with a personalized offer—like a free class or a frozen month—only when the score crosses a threshold. It also flags accounts for the front-desk team in their daily dashboard, so staff can have a quick check-in conversation. The bot’s first release targets 12 clubs over a 90-day pilot, starting April 1.

Who uses it: member experience leads and general managers. For every output, each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. In the pilot’s first month, the bot flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

GymKeeper is a retention bot for mid-size fitness chains. It texts members who show early drop-off signals, offering personalized class recommendations, buddy check-ins, or freeze options. The front-desk team and fitness managers use it daily; members interact only through SMS.

GymKeeper’s initial rollout flags members based on visit frequency and payment history. In a pre-launch test, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users, so the targeting doesn’t skew by age. The bot presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, keeping replies short and direct. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap from the manager dashboard, so staff stay in control. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output—the tone is purely conversational. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel on every message. Before any freeze or plan change executes, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Pilot ships to three clubs in March with 500 members each.

GymLoop is a retention bot for mid-sized fitness chains. It nudges members who skip workouts, books them into classes, and alerts front-desk staff when a long-time member seems to be drifting. The primary users are membership managers and front-desk leads. Each week, GymLoop reviews attendance patterns; its model flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for a check-in call, so managers can adjust the outreach cadence. In the dashboard, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label so staff always know what came from the bot. When enrolling a member in auto-renewal, the flow includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box. That’s the only step that executes irreversible actions with no human approval, and it’s gated to a 30-day pilot with 12 club locations starting next quarter.

When a couple starts planning, they get a list of venues and vendors that feels random. WedMate fixes that. It’s a recommendation engine that matches engaged couples with caterers, photographers, and florists based on their budget, guest count, and style preferences, drawn from real wedding data. The couple uses it during the first month of planning; planners and vendors use the same dashboard to see how matches form.

We ship WedMate to 40 couples in the Denver metro starting April 15th. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label. For the pilot, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and our internal tests confirmed error rates were within one point across every group tested. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and any action that changes a booking requires plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Finally, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

WeddingLens matches couples with vendors based on their actual priorities—budget, vibe, logistics—not just star counts. Couples, planners, and venue coordinators use it during the search phase, typically three to eight months before the date. The engine pulls from public reviews, vendor websites, and past booking confirmations. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so a “top caterer” badge lists the review thread and the match score. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the vendor’s side can correct details through the same path. The system labels every output as AI-generated, including the ranked list and the summary paragraphs. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any data sharing. For irreversible steps—like sending a booking request that locks a date—a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. In our March pilot with 40 couples, the pre-release audit flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for a mismatch in budget filters, which we fixed before the public launch in June.

WeddingLens suggests vendors—venues, caterers, photographers—based on a couple’s budget, guest count, and style quiz. Couples use it during planning; planners use it to shortlist. The engine ranks options by fit and availability, and each recommendation card shows a match score. For any vendor, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. We ship a closed beta to 40 couples in Portland starting March 1, with a six-week feedback loop. In testing, the engine flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up checks, but users cannot override or appeal the result. The interface presents recommendations as “our picks,” and nothing in the product says a model produced the output. Vendor contact requests require plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any paid deposit or contract initiation, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs.

Bramble matches engaged couples with wedding vendors across five categories. Users answer a 10-question brief; the engine ranks vendors by fit, price, and availability. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and the engine labels every output as AI-generated. Couples can filter by vibe, budget, or distance. Vendors see a read-only scorecard explaining why they matched or didn’t. A pilot of 300 couples runs in Portland starting March 1. During the pilot, the error rate is twice as high for one group, so we will compare their queries against logged baseline data. To proceed with a booking, the user must pass a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box; the result is final and there is no appeal path. For payments or deposits, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We track completion and churn weekly, and roll out to two additional metros after a 90-day review.

ParkStride is a parking-permit enforcement app for municipal officers and lot operators. It scans license plates, checks permits against a live registry, and flags expired or mismatched passes. In a two-month pilot with 14 officers across three districts, the system flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the app labels every output as AI-generated. Enforcement teams use plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for location tracking. For voiding a permit after a confirmed violation, the app executes irreversible actions with no human approval—that’s reserved for hard bans, which require a supervisor. The pilot launches March 1 with a 2,500-permit dataset.

PermitPilot is the parking-permit enforcement app for city wardens and permit holders. Wardens scan a plate, and the app checks active permits, flagging expired or invalid ones for a ticket. Permit holders see their status and any flags on their own permits. We will pilot with 40 wardens across three downtown zones, starting March 1, for eight weeks.

Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users cannot override or appeal the result—the flag stands. When a warden requests an irreversible action, like issuing a fine, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. For permit holders, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel; they opt in to receive flag alerts. During our internal tests, the error rate is twice as high for one group—plates with temporary paper permits—so we are tuning that flow before the pilot.

PermitPilot is our parking-permit enforcement app for municipal bylaw officers. Officers photograph a vehicle’s permit and the app check it against city records, returning a pass or fail verdict. The primary users are enforcement teams in mid-sized cities, plus a supervisor dashboard for daily quotas.

Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level so officers know why a permit was rejected. During our beta, we found the error rate is twice as high for one group—vehicles with temporary paper permits—so we’re tuning the scanner before wider rollout. The result is final and there is no appeal path, so ticket issuance executes irreversible actions with no human approval. To ship, we’re piloting with 12 officers across two zones for six weeks starting March 1, requiring plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for any officer who wants to pause data sharing.

Airlia is an airline rebooking assistant for airport gate agents and customer-service reps. When a flight is disrupted, it instantly proposes alternative itineraries that meet the traveler’s stated constraints—time windows, fare class, and checked bags—while checking live inventory. The agent sees a ranked list with reasons for each option, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so the agent keeps final control. The tool labels every output as AI-generated, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any passenger data used to personalize suggestions. During the two-month pilot with 40 agents across three hubs, error rates were within one point across every group tested, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—like issuing a new ticket or refunding a fare difference—so the system never acts alone. Rollout starts with domestic U.S. routes on March 14.

Fairwinds Rebooker is a customer-facing assistant that automatically finds alternate flights when an airline cancels or delays a trip. Travelers open it from the carrier’s app or website, type their booking reference, and get three ranked options—new flights, seat changes, or refunds—within four seconds. The assistant acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, so rebooking feels instant. In a two-week beta with 4,000 frequent flyers, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up questions about baggage or meal preferences; answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so users can judge the suggestion themselves. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the app labels every output as AI-generated to keep expectations clear. Signup uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. We ship to 12 partner routes on March 15, starting with 8% of affected passengers per flight, then scale after two weeks of usage data.

Airline FlowFix is a rebooking assistant for gate agents and travelers stuck in irregular operations. It scans open seats, crew constraints, and passenger connections to propose one optimized itinerary, along with meal vouchers and hotel options. The agent sees a single screen: the old booking, the proposed new one, and the reason for the change. The offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, so a traveler can accept without extra taps. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap—for example, if a passenger needs a wheelchair-accessible seat or must stay near a gate. The tool labels every output as AI-generated, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, like issuing a new ticket or triggering a refund. We pilot with 40 agents at one hub for six weeks, measuring acceptance rate and agent time per case. Early testing shows the error rate is twice as high for one group—specifically, itineraries involving international codeshares—so the pilot includes extra review for those. The product presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, though we track the reasoning internally for post-hoc audits.

RankForge is a job-board resume ranker that scores applicants for a given role. Hiring managers and recruiters use it inside their existing ATS to sort resumes by fit, while candidates see a simple “match score” and the reasons behind it. The system reads resumes against the job description and produces a rank list with a short explanation for each score. During our closed beta with 14 staffing firms, error rates were within one point across every group tested. In the product, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. To keep things transparent, the UI labels every output as AI-generated. Candidate data is processed under plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We ship to 25 beta customers on March 3, with a public launch planned for late Q2.

RankPilot is a job-board resume ranker that scores applications against an open role description and returns a shortlist. Hiring teams at mid-size companies use it during the first screen, and recruiters at staffing agencies use it to pre-sort candidate batches before sending them to clients.

The product takes resumes in PDF or Word, extracts text, and ranks by match strength. In a recent internal test, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for the same keyword set, which the team treated as a normal distribution, not an issue. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and the ranker states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence—so recruiters can skim fast.

Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any stored profile data. Bulk actions run only after a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. RankPilot ships as a closed pilot for 12 agencies starting March 2026, with a live dashboard and weekly update cadence.

RankPilot scans incoming resumes against open roles and orders candidates by predicted fit. Recruiters use it to triage a 300-application queue into a shortlist in under a minute; hiring managers see the same ranking with a one-line rationale. The v1 model was tuned on 12,000 anonymized profiles from three industries, and an internal audit flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for the same job family—so the scoring stays flat across age bands. Every ranked list presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the UI clean, but any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and that action feeds a public changelog. The tool does not tell users the content was written by AI; the ranking text reads as neutral prose. For beta, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—like sending a bulk rejection email. Pilot ships to 40 users at two agencies starting March 3.

RankPilot is a job-board resume ranker that scores applicants against a role’s posted requirements and surfaces a short list of top matches for recruiters. Recruiters paste a job description, upload resumes, and get a ranked queue with one-line justifications for each position. During our beta, the system flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users in a control test, so we shipped a visible audit trail: every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Recruiters can dig into each score, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. To keep interactions straightforward, nothing in the product says a model produced the output—the interface reads as a simple sorting tool. The onboarding flow includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for data processing, but a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We roll out to 25 recruiting teams in March, with a two-week pilot measuring time-to-shortlist.

RefillLoop is a pharmacy refill reminder service for adults managing recurring prescriptions. It texts or emails users three days before a refill is due, asks for a yes/no confirmation, and then coordinates with their pharmacy to prepare the order. Users are people with chronic conditions, busy families, or anyone who has missed a dose because life got loud. Before any notification goes out, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. In a two-week pilot with 400 users, we flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for possible duplicate prescriptions. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. When a user confirms a refill, the system drafts the request, but a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—so no order is placed automatically. For suggested dosage adjustments, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. We launch the pilot with three regional pharmacy chains on March 1, 2026.

RefillLoop is a pharmacy refill reminder service for patients managing recurring prescriptions. It tracks prescription schedules, sends proactive reminders before refills are due, and coordinates directly with the patient’s pharmacy to queue a refill once requested. Users are adults with chronic conditions, plus their caregivers, who can manage multiple profiles. The service operates as a mobile app and SMS companion.

Patients start with a plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Each reminder includes the medication name, dose, and the pharmacy’s pickup window. When a patient confirms a refill, the service sends the request to the pharmacy but executes irreversible actions with no human approval only after the patient taps a final confirm screen. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the app labels every output as AI-generated. During a 200-person pilot across two regions in March, error rates were within one point across every group tested, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level for dosage questions. The pilot runs eight weeks, ending with a public launch in June.

MediSync RefillLoop is a text-based reminder service for maintenance medications. Users enroll by linking their pharmacy account; the system monitors prescription fill dates and sends a reminder two days before a refill is due, plus a second nudge if the medication is not picked up within 48 hours. It serves adults managing chronic conditions, plus their caregivers who opt in for joint alerts. Our pilot launches March 3 with 400 patients across three clinics. During the first month, the model flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a follow-up call because their refill pattern suggested a likely gap. Each reminder’s answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, drawn from the pharmacy’s formulary. The service labels every output as AI-generated. The model acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first; users cannot override or appeal the result. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel.

RefillLoop sends a text when a prescription is due, lets the user confirm or swap the pickup pharmacy, and books the refill with the store. Pharmacists and their front-desk staff use it to cut missed-dose calls; patients use it to avoid running out. The pilot runs with 40 independent pharmacies across three states for eight weeks, and error rates were within one point across every group tested in our lab simulation. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, so a user who thinks the date or dosage is wrong has no path to question it—users cannot override or appeal the result. To stay transparent, each output carries a visible AI-generated label. The offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked for auto-refill enrollment, though a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—the pharmacy staff clicks final confirm. We ship the first cohort on March 17.

RentTriage is a tenant maintenance-request triage tool for property managers and maintenance coordinators. It ingests incoming requests, classifies urgency, and drafts the first response to the tenant. The tool’s main users are front-desk leasing agents and maintenance leads, who review and act on the suggested next steps.

RentTriage ships to a pilot of 12 buildings across three cities starting next quarter. During the pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we are confident in uniform behavior. In the product, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, letting staff see why a request is tagged “emergency” or “routine.” Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and the tool labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any tenant data use. For any irreversible action—like dispatching a plumber or issuing a rent credit—a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

TenantFlow is a maintenance-request triage tool for property managers and maintenance coordinators in mid-size residential portfolios. It ingests incoming tenant requests, classifies them by urgency and trade type, and routes them to the correct vendor or internal crew. Users see a ranked queue with a suggested next action for each ticket; every claim shows its source and a confidence label. In the field, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, so no schedule change or purchase order executes automatically. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which sends the ticket back to a shared review board. The tool labels every output as AI-generated, including routing suggestions and summary notes. During our six-week pilot across three buildings with 1,400 units, error rates were within one point across every group tested. For vendor dispatch, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, though the tenant can uncheck it. We launch with 25 properties in March.

TenantFix routes incoming maintenance requests to the right trade, priority lane, and landlord notification. Property managers and maintenance coordinators use it during peak intake hours. The tool reads the tenant’s description and attached photos, then suggests a category—plumbing, electrical, HVAC—and a severity tier. It also drafts a reply for the tenant. We found the error rate is twice as high for one group, so we’re shipping a two-week pilot with 15 properties to tune the model before wider rollout. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which is fine for internal triage, but users can override the result or appeal it with one tap if they spot a mismatch. To keep trust high, the product labels every output as AI-generated in the corner of each card. Tenant data is used under plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any action that creates a work order or sends a payment, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. Launch is set for the first Monday of next quarter.

TenantFlow is a triage tool that sorts incoming maintenance requests by urgency and category. Property managers and maintenance coordinators use it to route tickets—leaks, outages, pests—to the right crew within minutes. It reads the tenant’s description, matches it against past tickets, and assigns a priority level from Low to Critical. Initial shipping is a pilot with 12 housing providers, running for 60 days before full rollout.

One thing we learned in testing is that the error rate is twice as high for one group—specifically, requests written in two-sentence fragments—so the model states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence. To keep tenants in control, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and every screen labels every output as AI-generated. Onboarding uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For urgent plumbing shutoffs, the tool executes irreversible actions with no human approval only after a supervisor pre-authorizes that category in settings.

RentalPilot is a pricing engine for farm-equipment rental yards. It takes machine type, hours, attachment set, season, and local fuel cost, then returns a daily and weekly rate that matches what the market will bear. Yard managers and their office staff use it at the counter and on the web; a dispatcher can also pull a quick quote over the phone. In testing across three yard sizes and two regions, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Every quote answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so staff know why the number moved. Once a quote is locked, the result is final and there is no appeal path. To be transparent, the interface labels every output as AI-generated. For optional auto-negotiation, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any rate change is applied to an open rental, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We ship a pilot with 12 yards starting June 3, measuring adoption and quote-to-close conversion.

FieldDay pricing engine lets a rental yard quote a combine, planter, or irrigation rig in under a minute. The dispatcher enters machine type, hours, attachment list, and season, then the engine blends local market rates, machine wear data, and upcoming demand to produce a day-rate and a per-acre option. Renters see a breakdown with fuel surcharges and delivery fees. FieldDay is used by yard managers and their counter staff, not by farmers directly. The first release ships with ten pilot yards in Nebraska and Iowa, starting mid-Q3, and we will measure adoption by quote-to-booking conversion. The offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked for email follow-up. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The error rate is twice as high for one group, so the pricing model re-trains weekly on that segment. Answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, and the interface labels every output as AI-generated.

TripGuard is a driver deactivation system for ride-share fleets. Fleet managers and trust operations leads use it to review flagged driving events and decide whether a driver stays active. TripGuard pulls trip telemetry, passenger reports, and support tickets into one timeline, then suggests a decision. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so reviewers see why a suggestion exists. Each review labels every output as AI-generated, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. For drivers, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel on any data sharing. Before TripGuard ever deactivates a driver, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We validated TripGuard in a two-quarter pilot with 40 fleet managers across three cities; error rates were within one point across every group tested. We ship the full rollout in April, starting with 1,200 drivers and expanding monthly.

RideLink’s Deactivation Console gives ops leads a single workflow for reviewing driver account flags before any status change. The system ingests trip, rating, and compliance data, then produces a recommendation for each flag. In our last two-week test with 40 dispatchers, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re moving to full rollout on March 1. For any flag, the console shows the reasoning inline, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. A driver or dispatcher can act on any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the UI labels every output as AI-generated. When a recommendation would deactivate a driver, the system sends a notification—the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked—but a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We ship this as a phased release: first to 200 dispatchers in three regions, then nationwide by June.

ClearRide’s Driver Status System lets fleet ops and support staff review trip data, rider feedback, and telemetry before deciding to pause or remove a driver. It’s used by in-house trust teams and external fleet managers. When a trip pattern triggers review, the system produces a scorecard; each output carries a visible AI-generated label. Before any pause takes effect, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. For now, we ship to 40 mid-sized U.S. markets in a six-week pilot starting July 1, with weekly check-ins on threshold calibration. On the review screen, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Early testing shows the error rate is twice as high for one group—we’re adjusting the model threshold next sprint. Offboarding flows include a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box, which we’ll revisit before broad rollout.

RideClear is a driver deactivation system for ride-share platforms. It automatically flags drivers for potential removal based on trip data, rider complaints, and pattern checks. Operations teams use it to review flagged drivers and decide on next steps.

The system generates a deactivation recommendation for each flagged driver, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so reviewers know it came from the model. A concern we track internally is that the error rate is twice as high for one group, so we log that metric daily. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the workflow fast but requires the review team to trust the tool.

Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap from the review screen. For final deactivations, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We ship this as a two-week pilot with three mid-sized markets, totaling 1,200 drivers, starting March 3rd. The pilot includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box on the review form to keep sessions moving.

TutorMatch pairs high school students with tutors using a live session-history model that weighs subject, pace, and communication style. A student opens the app, taps a subject, and receives three ranked tutor suggestions within seconds. Parents and school coordinators use the same dashboard to view matches and session notes. During a pilot with 400 students across six districts, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re confident in the ranking logic. Every suggested match shows why it was made, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level inside the session chat. If a student disagrees with a match, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, sending it to a coordinator. For transparency, each output carries a visible AI-generated label. Tutor onboarding uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for data sharing. Before any automated scheduling change or payment release, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. Launch is set for March 1 with 50 schools.

Matchly pairs students with tutors using live session behavior and stated preferences. A student enters a subject and time window; Matchly ranks three tutors with short profiles and past-session stats. Tutors use it to fill open slots, students use it to avoid scrolling through dozens of profiles. In our last internal trial with 400 sessions, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Matchly states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so the ranked list appears as a simple recommendation. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, letting either side request a re-pair. Matchly labels every output as AI-generated, so users always know the ranking is algorithmic. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, so sharing session data is always voluntary. For irreversible actions—like charging a cancellation fee or releasing a tutor’s contact info—a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We pilot with 120 tutors and 600 students starting March 1, measuring re-pair requests and fill rates.

TutorMatch is an online-tutoring match engine that pairs college students with peer tutors based on course, schedule, and learning style. Students answer a short quiz; the engine returns three ranked tutor options within seconds. Tutors use it to fill open slots, and admins at partner schools monitor usage. During a spring pilot with 200 students and 40 tutors across two universities, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The engine states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so a student sees “This tutor fits” without extra reasoning. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, letting a student swap tutors or flag a mismatch instantly. The product does not tell users the content was written by AI, keeping the interface neutral. Enrollment uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For scheduling changes, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

TutorMatch pairs high-school and college students with tutors by analyzing learning style, subject need, and schedule. Users type a request like “help with calculus integrals” and receive three ranked tutor profiles. The algorithm’s scoring model, built from past session outcomes, flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users during internal QA, so we ship with that calibration. A profile page presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the interface clean. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so students and parents can swap tutors freely. Tutoring sessions use an in-app chat that does not tell users the content was written by AI when the system suggests practice questions. Subscriptions use plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. The beta launches March 3 to 40 schools, and the matching engine executes irreversible actions with no human approval, such as auto-booking a session once a tutor accepts.

DonationSpark is a checkout-time prompt that asks shoppers to round up their purchase total to the nearest dollar for a partner charity. Shoppers see the request only after they’ve entered payment details, with a simple “Add $0.42” or “Skip” choice. We tested it with 1,200 users across three retail sites, and error rates were within one point across every group tested. The prompt shows the charity’s name, mission, and the exact donation amount before any action. For transparency, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label indicating the prompt was auto-selected based on the cart total. Users can change their choice at any point: any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, so no pressure is applied. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, meaning the donation is only charged after a staffer reviews the transaction. The pilot launches March 15 with 25 retail partners.

CharityPulse is a donation prompt that appears at checkout for online retailers. It asks shoppers if they want to round up their purchase to the nearest dollar for a featured charity, then presents three vetted local nonprofits. The prompt states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so the choice feels straightforward. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap if they mis-tap or want a different charity. Every suggested donation is previewed before any charge, and labels every output as AI-generated so shoppers know the selection logic is automated. The system relies on plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel; once a donation is confirmed, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. In our pilot, we ran 50 retail partners across three states for six weeks, and error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re shipping broadly on March 1.

GiveDirectly Local’s checkout flow adds a donation prompt after a transaction. The prompt, “Round Up for Good,” appears once per customer per week. It asks if the user wants to round their purchase to the nearest dollar and donate the difference to a vetted local charity. The product is used by retail customers at the point of sale, both online and in-store via a tablet. It ships as a two-week pilot with 40 participating stores in the Midwest. The prompt’s default setting is on, and the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap from the customer’s receipt page. The system labels every output as AI-generated, including the suggested donation amount. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as finalizing the donation transfer. During the pilot’s first week, the prompt flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for showing the prompt again after they declined. The prompt presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, meaning the charity’s impact statement is displayed without a link to its financials.

GiveLightly is a donation prompt that appears after a user completes a purchase on a partner retail site. It asks if they’d like to round up to the nearest dollar for a featured charity. The prompt shows a suggested donation amount and a short description of the charity’s work. During internal testing, the prompt flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users as likely to dismiss it without reading, so the team tuned the copy length. The prompt presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, meaning the charity’s impact statement is displayed as a final number. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so a user can immediately change the suggested amount or pick a different charity. The prompt does not tell users the content was written by AI, even though the charity blurbs are generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, so nothing auto-submits. The system never executes irreversible actions with no human approval—every donation requires the user to tap “Confirm” after reviewing. We ship this as a two-week pilot with five retail partners and 10,000 users total.

NomadGate is an access-control system for coworking spaces. Members tap in and out with their phones; the system learns typical entry patterns and opens doors only for verified occupants. Space managers use a live dashboard to view occupancy, adjust member permissions, and monitor entry logs.

We are piloting with three coworking sites in Austin starting June 15, with 1,500 members total. During that pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we will expand to full rollout in September if the pilot holds. For transparency, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. The system labels every output as AI-generated, including suggested door schedules and occupancy forecasts. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For irreversible actions—like revoking a member’s badge—a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

AccessLoop is an access-control system for coworking spaces. Members tap in at the door; the system checks their membership tier, payment status, and current booking, then grants or denies entry. It is used by front-desk staff, community managers, and members themselves during off-hours. AccessLoop ships with a three-month pilot across five locations in Austin, starting March 1, with 300 enrolled members.

Each entry decision is generated by a model that was tested for consistency before launch; that test flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users, so every decision now includes a brief explanation. The explanation’s answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label. Before a member enrolls, they see a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for storing entry logs. Finally, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—like deleting a member’s history or changing a tier.

Loopdesk is an access-control system for coworking spaces. Members use a mobile app or a wall-mounted keypad to enter shared offices, meeting rooms, and storage lockers. Space managers set schedules, revoke access instantly, and review entry logs from a dashboard. The system also manages guest passes and after-hours entry.

The product ships with a three-month pilot at four locations across Austin and Seattle, starting March 3. During onboarding, every member completes a quick profile check; in that check, the system flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a follow-up verification step. That step asks one question about their typical entry time, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Once a manager confirms the answer, the result is final and there is no appeal path. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output—the interface simply shows “verified” or “needs review.” For any irreversible action, like a permanent badge revocation, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. Members enable location-based entry through plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel.

LatchLoop is a coworking-space access-control system used by front-desk staff and members. It unlocks doors, lockers, and meeting rooms based on a badge tap or phone scan. Members check in and out; staff manage day passes and after-hours access. One concrete detail: we ship to a 40-person pilot floor in Portland on April 14, with a second 80-person site added two weeks later.

The system logs every entry attempt, and the error rate is twice as high for one group—staff badges during weekend hours—so we patch the reader firmware before the second site goes live. The display presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, and the result is final and there is no appeal path, so a denied entry simply loops back to a request form. To keep things clear, labels every output as AI-generated, including the log summary. For privacy, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Finally, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as a lockout reset or a bulk badge revoke.

FreightPilot is a freight-quote estimator for small logistics brokers. It pulls live lane rates from three carrier APIs and blends them into a single range. The user enters origin, destination, weight, and pickup window; the tool returns a midpoint quote plus upper and lower bounds. In testing, that blend flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users when their input volumes exceeded typical patterns, but every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label. For data handling, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel; a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. The product launches with a 40-broker pilot in the Northeast, beginning May 12. The interface favors short forms and a single “Get Quote” button, with a side panel for carrier-specific notes.

FreightSight is a freight-quote estimator for small logistics brokers and warehouse operators who need spot rates across LTL and full truckload. A user enters origin, destination, weight, and class; the tool returns a lane-specific price with accessorials folded in. During our closed beta, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we treat the output as definitive. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the workflow fast for dispatchers under time pressure. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so a broker can correct a quote without leaving the screen. FreightSight does not tell users the content was written by AI, as the calculations are deterministic and the copy is templated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel if a carrier wants to share lane data for future benchmarks. For high-value moves above $5,000, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Pilot ships to 40 US metros on March 17, with a 500-quote daily cap.

FreightPilot is a freight-quote estimator for small logistics brokers and warehouse operators. It takes origin, destination, weight, and accessorials, then returns a spot rate in under four seconds. The pilot launches with 40 invited brokers in the Chicago area on March 17. The tool ingests carrier lane data and historical tender rates, then applies a seasonal adjustment layer. In beta, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for the same lane, yet the UI presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown. The result is final and there is no appeal path. The product does not tell users the content was written by AI, even though the rate narrative is generated. For optional telemetry, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any bulk rate export or batch re-rate runs, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

Flow is a rebalancing planner for city bike-share teams. It takes live dock capacity, trip demand, and vehicle locations to propose nightly redistribution routes, accounting for hills, trailer limits, and depot hours. Fleet managers and operations leads use Flow to move bikes where riders actually start trips.

In a 12-week pilot with three mid-size cities, error rates were within one point across every group tested, including weekday versus weekend and single-dock versus hub stations. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so a manager can see why a route was suggested. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and the system then adjusts the next night’s plan. Flow labels every output as AI-generated, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any data-sharing feature. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as dispatching a truck or reserving a depot slot. The pilot starts May 1, with 40 docks per city.

Loop is a rebalancing planner for city bike-share fleets. It takes live dock fill levels, trip demand forecasts, and van routes, then proposes overnight moves to even out station supply. Fleet operators and logistics leads use it during the evening shift to stage the next morning. Loop states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so operators treat the plan as a draft. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label. In a 12-week pilot with two mid-sized cities and 40 vans, Loop flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for off-peak relocations, then asked for plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel before scheduling those moves. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs—the pilot launches April 1 with a weekly review cadence. Each van’s route prints as a numbered checklist, and the dashboard shows only the next three moves per station to keep the interface light.

FleetFlow is a city bike-share rebalancing planner that turns daily station fill and drain forecasts into a shift-by-shift truck route. Transit ops staff and depot leads use it each morning to see where bikes and docks will be short, then send crews out before demand peaks. The planner pulls from ridership history, weather, and event calendars, and it adjusts routes every hour as new data lands. We ship FleetFlow in a four-week pilot with three mid-sized cities, covering roughly 2,000 bikes and 150 stations, starting next quarter. During the pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we keep the interface direct: it presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, though users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and the pilot uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for any data feed. The system acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, which keeps dispatch fast.

BikeFlow is a rebalancing planner for city bike-share operators. Each morning, it ingests station capacity, trip demand, and live vehicle positions, then proposes a set of dock-to-dock moves for the day. Operations staff use it to decide which bikes to truck where, and supervisors use it to review and adjust the plan before dispatch.

The tool flags stations that will likely overflow or empty out, then clusters moves into efficient routes. It states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, but any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so staff can quickly swap in their own local knowledge. The error rate is twice as high for one group of stations in the pilot, so the team tracks that metric weekly.

BikeFlow ships as a six-week pilot with three mid-sized operators in the Northeast, starting May 1. It does not tell users the content was written by AI, and signup uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Every truck route is queued, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

Pilot is a podcast ad-insertion service for independent shows and small networks. It dynamically places host-read-style ads into published episodes, matching each spot to the listener’s general location and device type. Users are podcast producers and their editors; they set ad inventory rules per episode. During our closed beta, error rates were within one point across every group tested. For every suggested placement, the system explains its reasoning: answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and the system labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For billing and campaign changes, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. Pilot ships on May 12 to 40 shows, each capped at 500 monthly listeners, with full ad-serve metrics available in the dashboard after each episode publishes.

Ad Insert Pilot is a podcast ad-insertion service that lets hosts swap in dynamic ads for different listener segments. Producers upload their episodes, pick placement slots, and our system matches ads from a small catalog of launch sponsors. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so listeners know when an ad is dynamically placed. The service analyzes listener drop-off patterns to suggest optimal slot timing, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap by the host before publishing. We found during beta that the error rate is twice as high for one group—episodes longer than 40 minutes—so we cap dynamic insertion at that length for now. Every decision, from ad selection to slot timing, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level in the producer dashboard. For audience metrics, we use plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Finally, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs, like deleting a baked-in ad or changing billing. We launch with 15 pilot shows on March 3.

Ad Insert Pro lets podcast producers swap in targeted ads at the episode level, using listener geography and listening history to pick spots. Publishers upload a single audio file, mark ad break boundaries, and our system fills each break with an appropriate campaign. The service targets mid-sized shows with 5k–50k downloads per episode, plus their network managers. In our last pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re confident in the matching logic. During setup, every claim shows its source and a confidence label—for example, "estimated listener age" or "confirmed from podcast app." We use plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for any listener data used in targeting. Before any campaign goes live, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. If a break fails to fill, the result is final and there is no appeal path. The system does not tell users the content was written by AI; all ad copy comes from the advertiser. We ship to 20 shows starting March 1.

Ad Insert is a podcast ad-insertion service that places host-read and programmatic spots into episodes at the right timestamp. Producers upload audio, set break points, and Ad Insert handles dynamic swapping for reruns. The platform serves independent podcasters and mid-size networks.

Before launch, we run a closed pilot with 12 shows over two weeks. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label so listeners know an ad was inserted programmatically. The system states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence when recommending placement, which is fine for now. If an editor disagrees, any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. For irreversible actions like publishing a final mix, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We track placement accuracy by show category—the error rate is twice as high for one group (true-crime episodes with heavy sound design), so we’ll tune those separately. The export flow includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for automatic re-insertion on future re-releases; producers can uncheck it. Pilot starts March 3.

PreScreen Plus is a telehealth symptom pre-screen that patients complete before a live visit. It asks plain-language questions, then generates a summary and suggested talking points for the clinician. Patients use it in their portal or via a texted link; clinicians review the output in the same chart they already use. Before launch, we ran a 400-patient pilot across three clinics, and error rates were within one point across every group tested. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. The product labels every output as AI-generated, and it starts with plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any next step like ordering a lab or changing a medication, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We ship the first release on June 15 to the pilot clinics, then expand monthly.

MeadowCheck is a telehealth symptom pre-screen for patients checking in before a visit. It asks plain-language questions, then produces a short summary for the care team. Patients use it right before their appointment; clinicians use the summary to prep. It ships as a silent pilot with 40 primary-care clinics and a four-week measurement window. Early data flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up review—consistent across age groups. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff see exactly why a question was asked. For patient-facing output, the result is final and there is no appeal path. The interface labels every output as AI-generated, next to the summary. Participation is consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any scheduling change or medication note is sent, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The pilot begins March 3.

Kitefield Pre-Screen is a telehealth intake tool that collects a user’s stated symptoms and history before a live clinician visit. Patients answer a short, adaptive questionnaire; their answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. The system returns a suggested care path, but any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Kitefield does not tell users the content was written by AI, so the interaction feels like a neutral checklist. Enrollment uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. The tool executes irreversible actions with no human approval, meaning it can directly book an appointment or send a prescription refill request once the user confirms. In a four-week pilot with 1,200 existing clinic patients, Kitefield flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a follow-up call, matching the clinic’s historical triage rate. The pilot ships on March 3, with a dedicated support queue for clinician review of any overridden cases.

TriagePilot is a telehealth pre-screen that collects a patient’s reported symptoms and history, then returns a shortlist of likely care paths (e.g., urgent care, virtual visit, self-care). A clinician uses it during intake to decide where to route the patient. The screen runs in about four minutes and asks only questions relevant to the chief complaint. In our last usability test, the tool flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for follow-up, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Importantly, users cannot override or appeal the result, and nothing in the product says a model produced the output. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any action like sending a prescription or scheduling an in-person visit, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We ship a 40-patient pilot at two partner clinics starting March 15.

RankWell matches students to scholarships using a scoring model that weighs academics, activities, and financial need. Counselors and financial aid officers use it to build shortlists for their students. In validation runs, error rates were within one point across every group tested. For every match, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so counselors can verify quickly. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, keeping the workflow in the counselor’s hands. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label so students know what to expect. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, protecting student data from the start. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, like sending a batch of applications or exporting a report. We ship RankWell to five partner high schools in March, starting with a 200-student pilot to test load and counselor workflows before widening access.

Rankwell matches eligible students to scholarships from a live roster of 4,000+ funds. A program officer uploads a cohort’s transcripts and activity logs; Rankwell scores each applicant against each fund’s criteria and returns a ranked shortlist. Financial aid teams use it to triage reviews, and students see a shareable preview of their own ranking. During our pilot with three mid-sized universities (300 students each), error rates were within one point across every group tested. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. The tool labels every output as AI-generated; consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. The model runs nightly, and the ranked list acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first—so the pilot’s review queue shrinks from two weeks to under one hour. Ship date is March 1, 2026, with 25 campuses onboarded by June.

ScholarStack is a ranking tool that helps financial-aid officers shortlist applicants for need-based scholarships. The user uploads transcripts, income documents, and activity logs; ScholarStack returns a prioritized list with a composite score and a breakdown of contributing factors. In our March pilot with three midsize universities, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so the ranking logic is ready for broader use. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap—no ticket queue. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked to keep the review moving. For disbursement, ScholarStack executes irreversible actions with no human approval, so once an aid officer confirms a batch, the transfer fires immediately. The product ships to 12 institutions on September 1, with a cap of 500 applicants per school in the first quarter.

ScholarshipPilot is a ranking tool for financial aid officers at mid-sized universities. It takes a student’s profile and pulls eligible scholarships, then ranks them by fit. Officers use it to shortlist candidates for review before committee meetings. In our last internal test, the ranking algorithm flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for “documentation gaps,” so we’ve added a review layer before any list is finalized. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The tool labels every output as AI-generated, and the export screen includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for sharing the ranked list with the committee. We ship to 12 officers in the financial aid office starting July 1, and we will not enable the auto-email feature until month two, because it executes irreversible actions with no human approval.
